query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of Ti (2–5 at%) to the equiatomic NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy increases grain-boundary cohesion and dislocation mobility, thereby improving its room-temperature ductility without significantly degrading the original high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy fabricated by vacuum arc melting and homogenized under standard conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small atomic fraction (2–5 at%) of Ti into the NbMoTaW composition via vacuum arc melting and subsequent homogenization.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests from ambient temperature up to ~1600 °C and heavy-ion irradiation at doses representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Solid solution modification of the single-phase BCC matrix by Ti, which enhances grain-boundary strength and dislocation processes.
generation.mechanism: Minor Ti additions strengthen grain boundaries and promote more uniform slip in the BCC lattice, increasing ductility without significantly altering the high-temperature mechanical properties or impairing the irradiation-induced defect evolution resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit higher ductility at room temperature, retain similar or slightly enhanced strength at ~1600 °C, and show comparable defect evolution under irradiation.
generation.baseline: Undoped NbMoTaW alloy with poor room-temperature ductility but excellent high-temperature strength and predicted irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: Exceeding 5 at% Ti may lead to secondary phase formation or a drop in high-temperature performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact Ti content that optimally balances ductility, high-temperature strength, and irradiation resistance must be verified experimentally, as processing routes and microstructure can influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of NbMoTaW alloys with 0, 2, and 5 at% Ti additions using identical melting and homogenization. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1600 °C, and subject samples to heavy-ion irradiation at high doses. Characterize defect morphologies, phases, and mechanical properties before and after irradiation.
measurements: Microstructure examination by TEM to assess irradiation-induced defects
Phase analysis by XRD or EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If added Ti does not yield enhanced tensile ductility at room temperature or if there is more than a 10–15% reduction in high-temperature strength or a pronounced loss in irradiation resistance compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
